stops.name: Zurich, Oberer Hirschengraben, the birth house
stops.campa: In the twelfth dawn of the year, in the surgeon Johann Baptist Pestalozzi's flat on the Oberer Hirschengraben, a son is born and named Johann Heinrich. Zurich lies under January frost, a city of guilds and pastors, of Zwingli's stern God and the lake's grey light. The family is old Locarnese stock, Protestant refugees of two centuries past: foreigners made burghers. No omen is recorded; the omen is the century itself, which will need a father for its orphans and has just received one.

stops.name: Zurich, the surgeon's deathbed and Babeli's vow
stops.campa: The father dies at thirty-three, and the boy is five. From the deathbed the surgeon calls the young servant Babeli and binds her by God and all mercy not to forsake his wife and children; the peasant girl gives her word and keeps it for a lifetime, refusing marriage, keeping the widow's narrow household on nothing. Heinrich grows up in a room of women, mother, Babeli, thrift and tenderness, knowing neither boys' games nor a man's hand, and the canon says: here the heart was made that would mother a nation's orphans.

stops.name: Höngg, the grandfather's parsonage
stops.campa: Summer after summer the boy is sent up the Limmat to Höngg, where his grandfather Andreas Pestalozzi has kept the village pulpit for half a century. He walks beside the old man on his rounds through cottages and spinning rooms, and for the first time sees the children of the poor: stunted at the loom, cheated of school, spent for wages before they are grown. In the parsonage garden the vocation is planted like a seed in the boy who does not yet know he carries it. The village children first seen are never afterward unseen.

stops.name: Zurich, Schola Abbatissana, the Latin school
stops.campa: At nine he enters the Latin school in the shadow of the Fraumünster. He is absent-minded, ink-stained, careless of his person: the schoolfellows call him Heiri Wunderli von Thorilikon, Harry Oddity of Foolstown, yet in the earthquake year, when masters and boys flee the shaking schoolroom, it is Heinrich who goes back alone up the trembling stair to carry out the forgotten books. The town laughs at the clumsy boy; the canon marks the first act of the pattern: where others run out, he goes in.

stops.name: Zurich, Collegium Carolinum at the Grossmünster, Bodmer's pupil
stops.campa: At seventeen he climbs to the Carolinum by the Grossmünster, the school of Zwingli's heirs, and comes under Johann Jakob Bodmer and Johann Jakob Breitinger, old men who teach Greek and Hebrew and something more dangerous: that the Swiss were once free peasants and might be again. Heinrich intends the pulpit, preaches once at Höngg, sticks fast in the Lord's Prayer, and comes down from the pulpit forever. The word he is to preach will not be spoken from above; it must be lived from below.

stops.name: Zurich, the Gerwe, the Patriots and Rousseau
stops.campa: In the guild room zur Gerwe the young men of Bodmer's circle found their Historical-Political Society: Lavater, Füssli, Bluntschli, Pestalozzi: the Patriots. They read Rousseau's Émile and the Contrat social as other ages read scripture; they fast on vegetables, harden their bodies, denounce corrupt bailiffs in print, and dream the regeneration of the fatherland. Heinrich, aflame, abandons theology for law, then law for the conviction that no folk is freed by paragraphs. Émile has told him where the revolution truly begins: in the child.

stops.name: Zurich, the Rathaus, three days under arrest
stops.campa: The Patriots go too far: a pamphlet against an extortionate bailiff, a comrade fled abroad, letters carried for the fugitive. The Council of Zurich seizes young Pestalozzi and holds him three days in custody, with a share of the investigation's costs for his ransom. The gates of every state career close on him with the cell door: no pulpit, no bar, no council seat will have a marked Patriot. The city that punishes him is doing the myth's work: it is driving him out of the professions and toward the land and the poor.

stops.name: Zurich, Neumarkt, Menalk's deathbed and Anna
stops.campa: His dearest friend Johann Kaspar Bluntschli, called Menalk among the Patriots, dies young, and from the deathbed charges Heinrich to shun politics and bind himself to a calm and steady course. Grief throws Pestalozzi together with Menalk's friend Anna Schulthess, a merchant's daughter eight years his elder. He courts her with the most honest love letter in the national canon, promising her not comfort but tears, debts, and a husband whose first bride is the fatherland and the poor. Against her parents' will, Anna says yes to exactly that.

stops.name: Kirchberg bei Bern, Tschiffeli's model farm
stops.campa: In autumn the townsman puts on the smock. At Kirchberg on the Emme he apprentices himself to Johann Rudolf Tschiffeli, the physiocrat whose model farm is the wonder of the Bernese enlightenment: madder and clover, new rotations, the creed that a nation's wealth rises out of its soil. Pestalozzi learns fields as he once learned Greek. After nine months he declares the apprenticeship complete, patience was never among his crops, and turns home burning to be a farmer of men. Tschiffeli, the canon notes, farms with capital; the pupil will farm with faith.

stops.name: The Birrfeld, the buying of the waste land
stops.campa: With a Zurich banker's five thousand gulden and his mother's small inheritance he buys some twenty hectares of the Birrfeld in the young canton's poorest corner: light, thirsty, stony ground that the peasants of Birr know better than the surveyors. He walks the field in the March wind and sees not what it is but what it must become: madder in rows, a house on the rise, the proof that scientific husbandry can lift the poor. He names the thing before it exists: Neuhof, the New Farm. The land, older than all enthusiasm, waits.

stops.name: Gebenstorf, the wedding
stops.campa: On the last day of September, in the village church of Gebenstorf where Aare, Reuss and Limmat gather toward their meeting, Heinrich Pestalozzi marries Anna Schulthess, quietly, far from Zurich, almost without guests, her family unreconciled. He is twenty-three, she thirty-one; between them they have his debts, her courage, and a field of stones. The three rivers joining below the church are the tradition's own emblem: two stubborn currents made one water, flowing from here downhill toward Birr, toward the sacrifice.

stops.name: Neuhof at Birr, the house on the Birrfeld
stops.campa: The manor house rises on the rise above Birr and the young family moves in: Heinrich, Anna, and the infant son Jean-Jacques, called Jaqueli, born 13 August 1770 and named for Rousseau as a knight names his son for his liege. Already the foundation is cracked: the banker, alarmed by whispers, has called in his loan; the madder does poorly in the light soil; harvests fail. Pestalozzi walks his mortgaged acres like a man who has read the end of the book and refuses it. The New Farm will fail as a farm so that it can become something the world has no name for yet.
